summary: Defines link relation types for navigating between a web resource and related version-control resources, such as past versions and working copies. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: These are labels on web links like earlier version or next version, so you can flip between old and new drafts.

questions: how to link to previous version of a web page
subtitle: Link types for web resources to navigate between versions, working copies, and version history.

tldr.problem: Websites and content management systems need standardized ways to link between versions of the same resource, such as older drafts, latest versions, and working copies.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines six link relation types that can appear in HTTP headers or Atom feeds: version-history, latest-version, working-copy, working-copy-of, predecessor-version, and successor-version.
tldr.outcome: These standard relation types enable clients and content management systems to navigate version-controlled resources without vendor-specific conventions.

today: RFC 5829 is an Informational standard that has not been obsoleted. These link relations are supported by content management systems and web frameworks that follow the Atom Publishing Protocol and other standards that use link relation types.

sections.title: Link Relations for Version Navigation
sections.content:
Web resources often exist under version control, where different versions, drafts, and working copies need to be linked together. This RFC defines a set of link relation types that standardize these relationships on the Web.

These relation types are used in the AtomPub bindings of Content Management Interoperability Services (CMIS), allowing content management systems and web servers to expose version links in HTTP headers and Atom feeds in an interoperable way.
sections.plainLanguage: When web pages or documents are being edited and updated, this gives them standard labels for all the different versions floating around.

sections.title: Version Control Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines key terminology: a versioned resource is placed under version control and often requires a checkout to modify and a checkin to finalize changes. A version history contains all versions of a resource. A working copy is a mutable resource used to create new versions. Predecessor and successor relations connect versions in sequence; merges may create versions with multiple predecessors.

These concepts align with versioning systems in WebDAV (Versioning Extensions to WebDAV, RFC 3253) and Java Content Repository (JCR), though the link relations are protocol-independent.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple: the original document, copies you edit, past versions, and the current 'live' version all have relationships you can follow.

sections.title: The Six Link Relations
sections.content:
version-history: points to a resource containing all versions. latest-version: points to the current or most recent version (on linear systems, the latest by timestamp; on branching systems, multiple latest-version links may exist). working-copy: from a versioned resource, points to an editable copy. working-copy-of: from a working copy, points back to the versioned resource it came from. predecessor-version: points to the prior version in the history. successor-version: points to the next version.

For systems with branching or merging, multiple links of the same type may exist on a single resource. This design allows clients to navigate version-controlled resources without prior knowledge of the server's versioning model.
sections.plainLanguage: Each relation is like a signpost: 'here is the history', 'here is the newest', 'here is the draft I'm editing', 'here is what came before', and 'here is what came next'.

sections.title: Registration and Standards
sections.content:
All six link relations have been registered with IANA under the Atom Syndication Format (RFC 4287). The registration records include the relation name, a description, expected display characteristics (undefined for all six, as they are for background processing), and security considerations.

Because these are standardized link relations, any server can use them, and any client implementing link relation support will recognize them without configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The official internet authorities have agreed on these names and what they mean, so they work everywhere.
